title: Mohnish Pabrai’s Interview session at The Diary of a CEO on July 13, 2025
summary: A wide-ranging interview on Pabrai's mental models for entrepreneurship and investing: cloning, zero-risk 'Dhandho' entrepreneurship, rapid prototyping with customers, cost discipline, recruiting and the givers/takers framework. On investing he stresses the Rule of 72, a long runway over starting capital or return, index funds or Berkshire for beginners, the punch-card and 'circle the wagons' idea, and confesses the Ferrari sale as his costliest mistake of omission.

ideas.idea: The world will easily accept three to five of the same thing, so cloning an existing business puts you 90-95% ahead of humanity.
ideas.detail: Bill Gates and Sam Walton were the greatest cloners: Word came from WordPerfect, Excel from Lotus, Bing from Google; Walmart cloned Sears and Kmart and Sam Walton claimed to have visited more retail stores than any human, learning even from a bad store's candle display. Howard Schultz cloned the Italian cafe for Starbucks.

ideas.idea: Entrepreneurs do not take risks; they do everything to minimize risk, and the truly risky thing is a nine-to-five job where you never get your music out.
ideas.detail: Bill Gates as a Harvard freshman had zero job-market value and could always return to finish his degree; Pabrai's own employer told him 'when your business fails, come back' with a promotion, so he had one free shot.

ideas.idea: Start your business while keeping your job, dropping your performance to just above firing level and converting free time into start-up hours.
ideas.detail: There are 168 hours in a week; keep sleep and the 40 hours of work, live close to work, and put in four hours on weekdays and 10 hours on weekends. He worked 7-9 am and 6 pm to midnight on TransTech; after nine months its cash flow exceeded his salary and he resigned.

ideas.idea: Never start a business to make money; the purpose of a business is to deliver an incredible product or service, and money is a side effect.
ideas.detail: The litmus test for whether you should do a start-up is that the start-up hours must be more exciting than your free time; Netflix and Instagram should feel painfully boring by comparison.

ideas.idea: Your original idea won't work because it came from the ivory tower between your ears; rapid prototyping with customers tells you what is 100% right.
ideas.detail: A Chicago bank IT boss kept forcing him back to slide 10 of his deck and gave him a purchase order; he expanded slide 10 into 20 slides and threw the rest away. Almost no business ends up with its originally conceived model. Google Glass failed because eyewear is personal, while Meta's Ray-Ban partnership has better odds.

ideas.idea: Costs are the one thing a business can always control, and disciplined cost-cutting like Walmart's and LVMH's is why their founders became the richest people.
ideas.detail: Sam Walton chose the seven-letter name Walmart partly to save on signage. Bernard Arnault runs LVMH tight, negotiating mind-blowing real estate deals despite being in luxury, and became Europe's wealthiest person.

ideas.idea: Replace capital with creative thinking: Richard Branson launched Virgin Atlantic with zero capital by leasing a spare Boeing 747.
ideas.detail: Branson called Boeing's switchboard about 30 times until leasing put him through; airlines collect ticket cash four months in advance and pay fuel and lease after the plane lands. Start-ups need less and less money and more brainpower over time.

ideas.idea: Sales is a numbers game: send 200 personalized letters a week, follow up relentlessly and track the ratios, because 98% saying no does not matter.
ideas.detail: He addressed CIOs by nicknames like 'Dear Dave' to confuse gatekeepers, called at 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 weeks, and never dropped anyone from the funnel until told to stop. TransTech grew from $400,000 in year one to $1.4 million, $3 million, and $15-17 million by year six or seven. His daughter got a hedge fund job by mailing 1,200 letters with a two-page stock pitch.

ideas.idea: His father's repeated bankruptcies taught him that offering gaps can be filled with no money, but leverage and over-aggressive growth destroy staying power.
ideas.detail: His father went bankrupt eight or nine times; at 11-12 Pabrai and his brother acted as his board figuring out how to survive one more day. At 16 he watched his father cold-call gold shops in Abu Dhabi and Doha, where the fifth shop bought and orders grew over repeat visits.

ideas.idea: Be a giver, not a taker or matcher: don't play math games on favors, always let the other guy get the better end, and the goodwill compounds.
ideas.detail: From Adam Grant's Givers and Takers: takers go nowhere and should be cut out of your life; givers become the most successful because the universe conspires to help them. The key is not doing it to get anything back.

ideas.idea: Recruiting is a founder's number one job: A players want A players, and the first B player starts the journey downhill.
ideas.detail: Elon Musk personally interviewed the first 3,000 SpaceX hires. Pabrai uses Caliper pre-employment testing because traits are hard-coded by genetics and the first five years of life. The three non-negotiables are intelligence, integrity and willingness to work hard; hire slow, fire fast, and firing fast matters more.

ideas.idea: Investing outcomes depend on starting capital, length of runway and rate of return, and if the runway is long enough the other two barely matter.
ideas.detail: The $23 paid for Manhattan in 1623 compounded at 7% (doubling every 10 years by the Rule of 72) would be $23 trillion by 2023, about one-sixth of total US household wealth of $150 trillion, more than the land is worth. Extend it back to 1523 and 2.3 cents does the same job.

ideas.idea: Spend less than you earn, save the first dollar not the last, and start at 22 so that money can compound for 50 years in a broad index.
ideas.detail: Put $5,000 of a $50,000 salary into savings first. $5,000 saved at 18 at 10% doubles seven times in 50 years, about 100x, to $500,000 at 68; add $5,000 every year and you end up with too much money without finding the next Nvidia.

ideas.idea: Beginners should just buy the S&P 500 index or Berkshire Hathaway as a set-it-and-forget-it holding and focus their energy on their own work.
ideas.detail: Open an account at Fidelity, Interactive Brokers or Robinhood; the S&P is somewhat overheated in mid-2025 and has long flat periods, but dollar-cost averaging over a long horizon is fine. BRK.B is like an index.

ideas.idea: Dhandho means a way of doing business where the downside is non-existent: heads I win, tails I don't lose much.
ideas.detail: Branson, Gates and Walton all built fortunes without taking risk. Everything in business is about risk reduction and free lunches, getting things done without capital.

ideas.idea: The Patels came to control 80% of US motels from 0.1% of the population by running family-staffed motels that undercut competitors on price.
ideas.detail: Expelled from Uganda by Idi Amin in the 1970s, they bought 10-20 room motels, lived in a couple of rooms, fired the staff, charged $19 against competitors' $25, ran higher occupancy, and bought the next motel for a nephew to run.

ideas.idea: 99.99% of start-ups are non-venture-backed, so ignore tech and look for 'offering gaps' the world needs but doesn't have.
ideas.detail: The barber who opens one day a week in a new town between two others charges $45 instead of $30 with no risk, doubling his business before competition neutralizes prices. Starbucks was an offering gap too.

ideas.idea: Every business starts without a moat; a moat is what makes it hard for competitors to take your customers, such as customers' habit of sticking with one barber.
ideas.detail: Founders find offering gaps, and sometimes a moat gets built, as with Visa and American Express, which persevere and scale.

ideas.idea: Apple is somewhat risky as an investment because everything emanated from Steve Jobs and nothing new has come out since he left.
ideas.detail: The smartphone brick form factor will change at some point and the replacement is more likely to come from someone in a garage than from Apple. Disney had to buy Pixar because there was no Disney anymore.

ideas.idea: 100% of businesses eventually go to zero, but IKEA's no-debt policy and rule that every new store must innovate show how to last far past the founder.
ideas.detail: IKEA's founder made decisions with a 500-year view; every store was built from retained earnings. Leverage is the single biggest reason businesses fail.

ideas.idea: Buffett's 20-punch card and the fact that 4% of listed stocks generate 90% of returns mean you should make few, thoughtful bets or simply own the index.
ideas.detail: Picking stocks gives about a one in 25 chance of landing one of the 4%; the index buys that 4% automatically. He declines to name specific stocks because it would hurt more than help.

ideas.idea: Day trading is not good; the brokers make all the money and there are no day traders in the Forbes 400.
ideas.detail: Robinhood will profit, not the young men drawn in by ads. Crypto is outside his competence so he does not touch it.

ideas.idea: Circle the wagons around a multibagger: only about 12 of Buffett's hundreds of investments moved the needle, and the key was never selling them.
ideas.detail: You cannot know before buying which stock will go 10x, 50x or 100x, but after owning it you may understand it well enough to know it is a great business that should not be sold.

ideas.idea: Mistakes of omission are far worse than the zeros; selling Ferrari after its 2015-2018 spin-off cost him about a billion dollars.
ideas.detail: In 2012 he bought Fiat Chrysler at a $5-6 billion valuation, ignoring that 80% of Ferrari was inside it. He made a couple of hundred million and sold after Ferrari listed; he owned roughly 1% of Ferrari, which now has a market cap near $100 billion.

ideas.idea: What is the point of billions if you are not happy? He asks daily how he wants to spend the day and maximizes what he loves rather than money.
ideas.detail: Right now that is golf; he nearly skipped the interview to play. Industrial psychologists told him he is a game player, which is why the letter-and-call funnel suited him.
